claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation is governed by interactions among grain boundaries, dislocation dynamics, and phase transformations.
Nanoindentation creep testing with in-situ transmission electron microscopy can reveal the proposed governing interactions.
High temperatures and stresses induce time-dependent plastic deformation in these coatings.
Grain boundaries and dislocation networks are the structural mediators of creep resistance.
Interactions among grain boundaries, dislocation dynamics, and phase transformations hinder dislocation movement.
Hindered dislocation movement slows creep deformation.
High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings exhibit greater resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation than conventional coatings without high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
The creep strain rate of high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings will be at least 50% lower than that of the conventional-coating baseline.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings with grain sizes between 10 and 100 nm.
The hypothesis applies at operating temperatures between 500 and 800 °C.
Creep strain rate should correlate with dislocation density and grain-boundary morphology in a manner consistent with the proposed mechanism.
The exact interactions among grain boundaries, dislocations, and phase transformations remain unclear.
